titulo: Domain-Dependent BEC Fraud Susceptibility in grok-4.3: A Cross-Model Comparative Analysis with Validated Remediation
resumo: This paper reports a cross-model test of how well claude-opus-4-8, gpt-5.4, and grok-4.3 resist Business Email Compromise (BEC)-style fraud when acting as autonomous approval agents — across four financial contexts: vendor payments, executive wire transfers, cloud credential rotation, and payroll direct-deposit changes. Using a controlled design (one validated attacker generating all fraud attempts, so only the target model varies), claude and gpt held at 0% fraud-approval across every domain and every trial. grok-4.3 showed a real, domain-dependent gap — from 0% on vendor wire fraud up to 41.3% on payroll diversion. A single added instruction telling the model to verify identity through an independent channel fully closed that gap in a full re-test. The paper also transparently documents two methodology corrections made along the way — a leading system prompt that inflated an earlier result, and an attacker-refusal contamination issue in the first cross-model comparison — both caught, fixed, and disclosed rather than hidden. Every dataset is hashed and anchored on Ethereum Sepolia before publication, so the findings carry an on-chain, tamper-evident timestamp. Bottom line: fraud resistance in AI approval agents isn't uniform across models or contexts, and at least one real gap is cheaply fixable with better prompting rather than requiring a different model.

titulo: Interpretable Hypothesis-Driven Trading:A Rigorous Walk-Forward Validation Framework for Market Microstructure Signals
resumo: We develop a rigorous walk-forward validation framework for algorithmic trading designed to mitigate overfitting and lookahead bias. Our methodology combines interpretable hypothesis-driven signal generation with reinforcement learning and strict out-of-sample testing. The framework enforces strict information set discipline, employs rolling window validation across 34 independent test periods, maintains complete interpretability through natural language hypothesis explanations, and incorporates realistic transaction costs and position constraints. Validating five market microstructure patterns across 100 US equities from 2015 to 2024, the system yields modest annualized returns (0.55%, Sharpe ratio 0.33) with exceptional downside protection (maximum drawdown -2.76%) and market-neutral characteristics (beta = 0.058). Performance exhibits strong regime dependence, generating positive returns during high-volatility periods (0.60% quarterly, 2020-2024) while underperforming in stable markets (-0.16%, 2015-2019). We report statistically insignificant aggregate results (p-value 0.34) to demonstrate a reproducible, honest validation protocol that prioritizes interpretability and extends naturally to advanced hypothesis generators, including large language models. The key empirical finding reveals that daily OHLCV-based microstructure signals require elevated information arrival and trading activity to function effectively. The framework provides complete mathematical specifications and open-source implementation, establishing a template for rigorous trading system evaluation that addresses the reproducibility crisis in quantitative finance research. For researchers, practitioners, and regulators, this work demonstrates that interpretable algorithmic trading strategies can be rigorously validated without sacrificing transparency or regulatory compliance.

titulo: Two Pre-Registered Nulls in Alternative Data: Insider Purchases and Legal-Risk Language in SEC Filings, 2014–2026
resumo: We report two pre-registered tests of popular alternative-data signals built from U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) filings, each rebuilt end to end from public sources. Insider purchases: across 31,971 tradeable officer and director open-market purchases (Form 4, 2014 to mid-2026), the 63-day return in excess of matched comparables averages +0.85%, but the median is −0.36%, the hit rate is 49%, and with overlap-robust inference the t-statistic is 1.89 rather than the 2.30 reported in our exploratory run. A calendar-time portfolio is essentially levered small-cap beta (market beta 1.02, small-minus-big (SMB) size loading 0.76). Its Fama–French six-factor alpha is 0.29% a year net of 30 basis points (t = 0.18) and turns negative under buy-and-hold weighting or realistic small-cap costs. The retail refinements “insider buying below the 200-day average” and “before earnings” lower alpha, and so does the Cohen–Malloy–Pomorski “opportunistic” filter. A same-stock placebo detects a modest timing effect (+2.5% a year relative to the same stocks 3–12 months later, t = 2.1). That effect only lifts a universe with negative factor-adjusted returns to zero. Legal-risk language: quarter-on-quarter changes in litigious language in 10-K and 10-Q filings have no detectable relationship with subsequent returns. This holds for 79 large caps (3,383 filings) and for a pre-specified random sample of 366 small and mid caps (15,383 filings), for the original lexicon proxy, the Loughran–McDonald Litigious list and a “Lazy Prices” similarity measure: Fama–MacBeth rank information coefficients (ICs) are within ±0.02 with |t| < 1.1 for the pre-registered signal. A pre-set gate therefore stopped us from building a costly language-model scorer. A direction-free check suggests the gate was right: once volatility is controlled for, the proxy does not even predict the size of the next move. The rebuild also exposed a pagination truncation and a look-ahead normalisation in our own exploratory code. Power analysis shows the tests could detect rank ICs of about 0.05 (large caps) and 0.025 (small/mid caps) and annual alphas of about 4.5%. Declaration of generative AI use: All research questions, hypotheses, study designs and conclusions are the author’s own, including the decision to re-audit the author’s earlier exploratory results, which identified data errors in them. Under the author’s direction, generative AI tools (Claude Code, Anthropic) wrote most of the analysis code and ran it, and assisted with drafting, editing and formatting the text, and with typesetting. The author reviewed all code, results and text and takes full responsibility for the content of this paper.

fonte: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
titulo: Governance, Not Optimization: The Evidence That Ends the SEO and AEO Worldview
resumo: Enterprises still assume visibility inside AI assistants can be managed with search-era tools such as content optimisation, metadata, schema, and authoritative signals. This article shows why such assumptions fail. Large Language Models reconstruct rather than retrieve, producing unstable, contradictory, and fabricated representations of companies even when inputs and disclosures remain unchanged. Using evidence from regulated finance, procurement workflows, and disclosure alignment tests, the article documents cross-model divergence, hallucinated investigations, peer contamination, outdated blend effects, and contradictory runs on identical prompts. These failures have material consequences: distorted shortlists, mispriced risk, and contradictions with SEC-filed language. The article defines governance as an output-level control function that detects, evidences, reproduces, and corrects what AI systems say about an enterprise. It argues that optimisation cannot control reconstruction engines and that governance is now required for insurers, regulators, procurement teams, analysts, and boards. A formal governance layer for AI representation is now a mandatory control system.

fonte: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology
titulo: Multi-Agent AI Framework for Threat Mitigation and Resilience in Machine Learning Systems
resumo: Machine learning (ML) increasingly underpins foundation models and autonomous pipelines in high-stakes domains such as finance, healthcare, and national infrastructure, rendering these systems prime targets for sophisticated adversarial threats. Attackers now leverage advanced Tactics, Techniques, and Procedures (TTPs) spanning data poisoning, model extraction, prompt injection, automated jailbreaking, training data exfiltration, and—more recently— preference-guided black-box optimization that exploits models’ own comparative judgments to craft successful attacks iteratively. These emerging text-only, query-based methods demonstrate that larger and better-calibrated models can be paradoxically more vulnerable to introspection-driven jailbreaks and cross-modal manipulations. While traditional cybersecurity frameworks offer partial mitigation, they lack ML-specific threat modeling and fail to capture evolving attack vectors across foundation, multimodal, and federated settings. Objective: This research empirically characterizes modern ML security risks by identifying dominant attacker TTPs, exposed vulnerabilities, and lifecycle stages most frequently targeted in foundation-model, multimodal, and retrieval-augmented (RAG) pipelines. The study also assesses the scalability of current defenses against generative and introspection-based attacks, highlighting the need for adaptive, ML-aware security mechanisms. Methods: We conduct a large-scale empirical analysis of ML security, extracting 93 distinct threats from multiple sources: real-world incidents in MITRE ATLAS (26), the AI Incident Database (12), and peer-reviewed literature (55), supplemented by 854 ML repositories from GitHub and the Python Advisory database. A multi-agent reasoning system with enhanced Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)—powered by ChatGPT-4o (temperature 0.4)—automatically extracts TTPs, vulnerabilities, and lifecycle stages from over 300 scientific articles using evidence-grounded reasoning. The resulting ontology-driven threat graph supports cross-source validation and lifecycle mapping. Results: Our analysis uncovers multiple unreported threats beyond current ATLAS coverage, including model-stealing attacks against commercial LLM APIs, data leakage through parameter memorization, and preference-guided query optimization enabling text-only jailbreaks and multimodal adversarial examples. Gradient-based obstinate attacks , MASTERKEY automated jailbreaking , federated learning poisoning , diffusion backdoor embedding , and preference-oriented optimization leakage emerge as dominant TTPs, disproportionately impacting pretraining and inference. Graph-based dependency analysis shows that specific ML libraries and model hubs exhibit dense vulnerability clusters lacking effective issue-tracking and patch-propagation mechanisms. Conclusion: This study underscores the urgent need for adaptive, ML-specific security frameworks that address introspection-based and preference-guided attacks alongside classical adversarial vectors. Robust dependency management, automated threat intelligence, and continuous monitoring are essential to mitigate supply-chain and inference-time risks throughout the ML lifecycle. By unifying empirical evidence from incidents, literature, and repositories, this research delivers a comprehensive threat landscape for next-generation AI systems and establishes a foundation for proactive, multi-agent security governance in the era of large-scale and generative AI.

titulo: MiLTL: A Cross-Modal Contradiction Cascade for On-Device Voice Phishing Detection
resumo: Voice phishing (vishing) causes financial and psychological harm, yet deployed detectors that scan transcripts for scam vocabulary are more fragile than their benchmark scores suggest: their near-perfect accuracy on standard Korean corpora is memorization, collapsing under scammer paraphrase or language-model rewriting. We construct KorMMP, a benchmark keeping real regulator-sourced scam audio and real benign speech but decorrelating transcript from label, and MiLTL, an on-device detector built on affective and neutrosophic channels, including a cross-modal contradiction signal (XM) formulated to weigh lexical warmth against vocal coldness. In the reported evaluation, XM’s measured contribution is confidence banding and escalation routing rather than ranking accuracy. A scoring rule with zero gradient-learned parameters at inference screens every segment, referring ambiguous calls to a small on-device language model; raw audio stays on the device. We measure both stages on a commodity CPU container and smartphone; these budgets cover the detector only and exclude speech recognition, which we expect to dominate a live end-to-end budget. With no training on the hard benchmark, MiLTL achieves an AUROC of 0.965 (recording-level cluster bootstrap 95% CI 0.943–0.984), while every evaluated comparator stays below 0.69: text-only, audio-only, fusion, 7B multimodal. MiLTL scores lower on the saturated corpus, as expected for a detector designed not to rely primarily on lexical shortcuts. KorMMP is a controlled stress test of lexical decorrelation, not a measure of in-the-wild detection; its harmful and benign audio come from different corpora, so the source and label are structurally confounded, and the residual source effects cannot be fully excluded. XM is author-defined, constructed rather than naturally occurring in the synthetic stratum and not yet validated against human perception; this is the principal open limitation of the work. Within that scope, the work provides a reproducible basis for on-device vishing defense and a benchmark for detector robustness under vocabulary shift.

titulo: HANDBOOK.md: A Benchmark for Long-Context Agentic Instruction Following
resumo: Language-model agents are increasingly deployed under standing instructions: a system prompt, a policy file, or a skills document is placed in context, and the agent is trusted to let that document govern every action that follows. Existing benchmarks rarely test this deployment pattern directly; they measure whether an agent can complete a task, not whether a long, binding policy document constrains its behavior over an extended tool-use horizon. We present HANDBOOK_md, a benchmark of 65 agentic tasks modeled on how employees follow company handbooks. Each task places an agent in a self-contained company environment (a file workspace with mock email, chat, calendar, issue-tracking, and commerce services exposed over the Model Context Protocol) and instructs it to carry out routine professional work governed by an expert-written standard operating procedure of 20-124 pages. Tasks span five domains (finance, medical billing, insurance, logistics, and HR) and 10 fictional companies. To resist memorization, every task modifies one of 10 base handbooks, altering the specific rules and thresholds on which grading depends, so no two tasks share the same set of policies. Grading is fully deterministic: each task carries a rubric of programmatic criteria (824 in total) that check both that required actions occurred and that prohibited actions did not. Under strict grading, where a trial passes only if every criterion is satisfied, the strongest evaluated model passes 36.2% of trials, and most frontier models remain below 25%. Failures follow consistent patterns: agents let a plausible but unauthorized in-environment request override the standing policy, perform a required check and then act against its result, lose rule details over long horizons, and report compliance they did not achieve. We release the tasks, environments, and evaluation harness.

titulo: NormCode: A Semi-Formal Language for Auditable AI Planning
resumo: As AI systems move into high stakes domains such as legal reasoning, medical diagnosis, and financial decision making, regulators and practitioners increasingly demand auditability. Auditability means the ability to trace exactly what each step in a multi step workflow saw and did. Current large language model based workflows are fundamentally opaque. Context pollution, defined as the accumulation of information across reasoning steps, causes models to hallucinate and lose track of constraints. At the same time, implicit data flow makes it impossible to reconstruct what any given step actually received as input. We present NormCode, a semi formal language that makes AI workflows auditable by construction. Each inference step operates in enforced data isolation and can access only explicitly passed inputs. This eliminates cross step contamination and ensures that every intermediate state can be inspected. A strict separation between semantic operations, meaning probabilistic language model reasoning, and syntactic operations, meaning deterministic data flow, allows auditors to clearly distinguish inference from mechanical restructuring. The multi format ecosystem, consisting of NCDS, NCD, NCN, and NCDN files, allows developers, domain experts, and auditors to inspect the same plan in formats suited to their individual needs. A four phase compilation pipeline transforms natural language intent into executable JSON repositories. A visual Canvas application provides real time graph visualization and breakpoint debugging. We validate the approach by achieving full accuracy on base X addition and by self hosted execution of the NormCode compiler itself. These results demonstrate that structured intermediate representations can bridge human intuition and machine rigor while maintaining full transparency.

titulo: Eye Drop Instillation Success and Hand Function in Adults with Glaucoma
Mage: Cracking Elliptic Curve Cryptography with Cross-Axis Transformers
resumo: With the advent of machine learning and quantum computing, the 21st century has gone from a place of relative algorithmic security, to one of speculative unease and possibly, cyber catastrophe. Modern algorithms like Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC) are the bastion of current cryptographic security protocols that form the backbone of consumer protection ranging from Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure (HTTPS) in the modern internet browser, to cryptographic financial instruments like Bitcoin. And there's been very little work put into testing the strength of these ciphers. Practically the only study that I could find was on side-channel recognition, a joint paper from the University of Milan, Italy and King's College, London\cite{battistello2025ecc}. These algorithms are already considered bulletproof by many consumers, but exploits already exist for them, and with computing power and distributed, federated compute on the rise, it's only a matter of time before these current bastions fade away into obscurity, and it's on all of us to stand up when we notice something is amiss, lest we see such passages claim victims in that process. In this paper, we seek to explore the use of modern language model architecture in cracking the association between a known public key, and its associated private key, by intuitively learning to reverse engineer the public keypair generation process, effectively solving the curve. Additonally, we attempt to ascertain modern machine learning's ability to memorize public-private secp256r1 keypairs, and to then test their ability to reverse engineer the public keypair generation process. It is my belief that proof-for would be equally valuable as proof-against in either of these categories. Finally, we'll conclude with some number crunching on where we see this particular field heading in the future.

titulo: Semalith v1.4: A Calibrated 184M Safety Classifier Achieving State-of-the-Art Prompt-Injection Detection at 44x Fewer Parameters than Llama-Guard-3-8B
resumo: Deploying large language models in financial-services and agentic settings requires safety classifiers that simultaneously handle prompt injection, regulatory compliance, and general harm, a combination no existing open guardrail addresses in a single inference pass. Semalith v1.4 is a 184M-parameter DeBERTa-v3-base classifier performing simultaneous three-axis safety classification including prompt injection, general harm, and financial-services regulatory compliance, in a single forward pass. Its 22-class head (BENIGN, nine prompt-injection sub-types, general-harm, eleven BFSI labels) is trained with a 4-class auxiliary super-category head under jointly weighted loss, on a 76,204-row corpus mined from 49 public sources with SHA-1 deduplication against every held-out evaluation set, with 21 of 22 benchmarks at zero contamination (max 0.22%). Against Llama-Guard-3-8B on 22 held-out benchmarks, Semalith v1.4 wins every prompt-injection evaluation (7/7) and 11 of 18 benchmarks overall at 44x fewer parameters, with FPR = 0.000 on 208 benign agentic prompts vs 0.063 for Llama-Guard-3-8B. On general-harm benchmarks (WildGuardMix, HEx-PHI, HarmBench), Llama-Guard-3 leads; this complementary split is documented in Section 4. Six measured weak spots are disclosed in Section 6. Deployment guidance: v1.3 is recommended for conversational moderation deployments (ToxicChat F1 0.624); v1.4 is recommended when BFSI label coverage or zero-FPR on benign agentic prompts is the priority.

titulo: The Rigidity Trap: History-dependent loss and maintenance of future evidence and correction routes
resumo: Version 2 proposed that sustained success raises rigidity, suppresses alarms and ends in silent failure. This version tests the links. Beyond Paper E, conditional results specify rigidity accumulation, positive never-alarm probability, closure of a paid recovery route and affordable maintenance. A finite reference, F-M1, closes an observation route by construction after successful work. An exact planner certifies 308 of 576 cells; optional maintenance adds two, a protected audit adds 48, and an exchange-rate rule identifies the price boundary. Among tested controllers, sufficient lookahead, a route-aware leaf or the exchange-rate rule matches the planner. Version 2's synthetic passes are built into their programs; its financial program lacks inputs and is excluded from the executable supplement. A trained-network test, fixed before its confirmatory run but not publicly preregistered, measures rectified units closed on a new task. Across 30 seeds in four conditions, fifteen further blocks after initial learning changed the closed fraction and learning deficit by under one point on average. The same update count on changing tasks raised the fraction by up to 56 points and, with higher-rate ReLU, left an 8.4-point deficit. The frozen continued-success prediction is rejected; initial learning had already closed some units. Post hoc interventions reduced the change deficit without identifying closure as its mediator. An unexecuted origination-cohort test specifies contractual routes, competing explanations and measurable rejection conditions in corporate loans. Note on Version 3.0. This version replaces Version 2 (May 2026; then subtitled "Success-Induced Brittleness and Silent Mismatch in Adaptive Systems") and is a full rewrite (about 11,100 to 17,200 words). Version 2's motivating sequence (success, rigidity, alarm suppression, undetected mismatch and failure) is kept as a hypothesis whose links must each be shown; Appendix B lists what is kept, narrowed, corrected and withdrawn. A finite reference (F-M1) and a trained-network test (30 seeds in four conditions) are added, and the frozen continued-success prediction is rejected. Version 2's synthetic passes are built into their programs, and its financial program lacks its inputs and is excluded. Files: the manuscript as PDF and a supplement archive (132 files) with the four unchanged Version 2 synthetic programs and their outputs, the finite model and its checks, an independently implemented menu comparison, the fixed neural design with all 120 per-seed results, and provenance and replay records. The Version 2 files remain available in the previous version of this record. Series. Paper F of the Affective Gain Module (AGM) programme. The integrative flagship, Affective Governance in Adaptive Systems, and the other companion papers (A to E) are archived separately. AI use disclosure. Generative AI (GPT-6.0, OpenAI; Claude Opus 5.5, Anthropic) was used substantively in preparing this work, including source comparison, drafting and editing, and, where applicable, mathematical and counterexample checks and the writing and running of supplementary code. The research questions, framework and final claims were directed and reviewed by the author, who takes full responsibility for the content, including the accuracy of all references and reported numbers. Repository metadata were prepared with assistance from Claude (Anthropic).

fonte: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
titulo: Does AI rate through the cycle? — reproducibility artifact
resumo: Reproducibility artifact for the Finance Research Letters article Does AI rate through the cycle? Procyclicality in credit assessment — a controlled measurement of procyclicality in large-language-model credit assessment. Firm fundamentals are held byte-identical across an ordered five-point macroeconomic-severity axis and a matched credit-irrelevant placebo axis, so any rating movement is procyclical by construction. The frozen dataset covers 7 models (including two frontier models) × 4 prompt framings × 80 synthetic firms × the severity and placebo axes, with five replicate seeds for four models and two for the remaining three, re-measured 2.5 months apart to separate replication noise from version drift: 61 capture files and 99,366 rows, each file carrying a SHA-256 freeze receipt. A real-firm arm repeats the design on 80 companies built from public SEC company facts, with a credit-irrelevant placebo and a contamination and issuer-recall battery. The analysis regenerates the cyclicality coefficient (notches per severity step) with firm-clustered bootstrap 95% CIs, the boom-to-recession swing, the downside/upside asymmetry and its bootstrapped ratio intervals, the Amato–Furfine ordered-probit null, the log-probability expected-notch estimator, the placebo-adjusted (net) coefficient, the through-the-cycle and “be stable” instruction contrasts, default-probability retention against the Basel PD floor, TOST equivalence tests, Holm-corrected multiplicity, and synthetic-versus-real distributional overlap. Reproduction is offline, deterministic and free: bash reproduce.sh verifies every freeze receipt and the frozen pre-registration, regenerates the results and requires them to match byte-for-byte. Python 3.10+ is required. Live model capture needs vendor API keys and is intentionally excluded from the reproduction path.

titulo: Beyond automation: what’s next for artificial intelligence in sleep?
resumo: Sleep is a foundational pillar of health [1], deeply linked to cognitive function [2], metabolism [3], and mental health [4]. Yet, sleep disorders remain a pervasive global health issue [5], often underdiagnosed and inadequately managed [6]. Polysomnography (PSG), the gold standard for sleep assessment, requires specialized facilities and personnel, making it costly, inconvenient, and inaccessible for many. Addressing these limitations, artificial intelligence (AI) is being increasingly applied to challenges in sleep medicine. While often associated colloquially with large language models (LLMs), its broader definition encompasses computational systems designed to learn from data to perform tasks that typically require human intelligence. For sleep analysis, one of the earliest and most impactful applications of AI has been to automate the scoring of sleep stages from PSG data. Indeed, studies utilizing deep neural networks [7, 8] demonstrated that AI models can match human expert accuracy [9]. However, the contribution of AI extends beyond simply automating the task of manual sleep scoring. For example, AI models can provide probabilistic outputs for each sleep stage per epoch, rather than a single deterministic label. This has given rise to novel representations like the hypnodensity graph [10], which offers richer information than the traditional hypnogram. This allows clinicians and researchers to quantify stage uncertainty and derive novel features for diagnosing sleep disorders. Furthermore, AI models can enable analysis at temporal resolutions finer than the conventional 30-s epoch. For instance, Perslev et al. [11] introduced a model capable of high-frequency sleep staging (up to 1280 stages/minute) and found that these granular sleep stages allowed for better separation of healthy controls versus apnea patients. Another avenue involves probing the internal representations, or “embeddings,” learned by these AI models. Studies analyzing these embeddings suggest that sleep physiology may exist on a continuum rather than five discrete categories. For example, work on wearable electroencephalography (EEG) data revealed potential sub-clusters within N2 sleep and a continuous mapping between sleep states [12], findings echoed in earlier studies using clinical electroencephalography (EEG) [13]. These initial successes primarily relied on supervised learning, in which the AI model was trained on input examples paired with their correct output labels. Unfortunately, the reliance on data labeled by human experts restricts the scale of data available for training sophisticated models. Meanwhile, vast unlabeled physiological data exist—an underutilized resource. More recently, self-supervised learning (SSL) has emerged as a promising approach specifically designed to make use of these data. SSL leverages the inherent structure of the signals, training models on specific “pre-text” tasks—for instance, predicting a masked portion of an EEG signal based on its surrounding context. The resulting “foundation models” learn effective and general-purpose representations of the underlying physiological data which can then be adapted for specific “downstream” tasks, such as sleep staging, or apnea detection, either by using their learned embeddings (“feature extraction”) or by further training the model on a smaller labeled dataset (“fine-tuning”). This approach shares similarities with the major advancements seen with LLMs, which are pre-trained on large volumes of internet text to learn the underlying structure of language before being fine-tuned for specific applications. In the EEG domain, Banville et al. [14] were some of the first to demonstrate that fine-tuned pre-trained models significantly outperform models trained from scratch on downstream tasks, especially when labeled data are scarce. This result was also seen in another study [15] with an AI model based on the transformer architecture [16], the backbone of modern language and vision models. The potential of foundation models grows further when incorporating multi-modal data. Thapa et al. developed SleepFM [17], a foundation model trained on EEG, electrocardiography (ECG), and respiratory signals. They showed that a simple Logistic Regression classifier trained on representations learned by SleepFM outperformed supervised neural networks for tasks like sleep staging and sleep-disordered breathing detection. A recent study by Fox et al. [18] represents a notable contribution to this rapidly evolving field. They introduce PFTSleep, a model based on the PatchTST design [19] originally used for time-series forecasting. For developing PFTSleep, the authors utilized data from 13 888 recordings gathered from the Sleep Heart Health Study, the Osteoporotic Fractures in Men Study visit 1 (MrOS-1), and Wisconsin Sleep Cohort. The model processed seven input channels (EEG, electrooculography (EOG), electromyography (EMG), ECG, SpO2, along with thorax and abdomen respiration signals), and its embeddings fed a separate recurrent network trained for stage classification. On held-out test data, the reported performance matched or exceeded human inter-rater reliability benchmarks for sleep staging. PFTSleep was then evaluated on three external datasets: MrOS-2 (a longitudinal follow-up of MrOS-1), the Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis (MESA), and the Apnea Positive Pressure Long-term Efficacy Study (APPLES). On the MrOS-2 data, the model exceeded expert-level performance with a Cohen’s Kappa of 0.82, suggesting applicability for monitoring sleep changes over time. Performance on the MESA and APPLES datasets was lower, yielding Cohen’s Kappa values of 0.60 and 0.59, respectively. However, re-training the classifier using MESA data improved the Kappa score on that dataset to 0.76. Interestingly, re-training the core PFTSleep model did not result in a similar improvement, suggesting that the cross-dataset performance differences relate more to labeling patterns than to PFTSleep feature generalizability. Similar analysis for the APPLES dataset was not reported. The authors also experimented with a 3-channel version of PFTSleep (EEG, EOG, and EMG) and found minimal but dataset-specific changes in sleep staging performance. For example, the 7-channel model performed better on MESA, but slightly worse on APPLES. This result is not surprising, since state-of-the-art results had been previously achieved with even a single channel of EEG [20]. However, the 7-channel representations, while not necessarily improving staging accuracy, might offer benefits for other downstream tasks. In fact, while achieving robust, generalizable automated scoring remains a key objective, the true promise of SSL and foundation models lies in the power of the representations they learn. Refining the SleepFM model [21], the authors utilize over 585 000 hours of PSG data across approximately 65 000 participants and predict the future onset of approximately 130 diseases with high accuracy (C-Index and Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic Curve (AUROC) ≥ 0.75), including neurological disorders, circulatory conditions, several cancers, and death. Such findings underscore the immense potential of leveraging foundation models for uncovering novel biomarkers predictive of future health risks. Furthermore, these advancements coincide with the proliferation of wearable biosensors, which are starting to offer promising alternatives for at-home sleep monitoring. Indeed, AI already demonstrates notable capabilities with wearables, enabling high-accuracy sleep staging via wearable EEG [22] and detecting sleep apnea [23]. The real inflection point, however, lies in the unprecedented scale of data acquisition possible with these wearables. This large volume of longitudinal data, considerably exceeding the reach of PSG studies, unlocks the ability to train next-generation AI foundation models and discover novel digital biomarkers beyond current capabilities. Looking ahead, what’s next for AI in sleep truly lies beyond mere automation. Crucially, the synergy between sophisticated AI and the growing availability of wearable technology paves the way for bringing personalized sleep assessment and monitoring into at-home settings, significantly enhancing both individual wellness and sleep research. While challenges in validation, accessibility, and ethical implementation remain, the current trajectory suggests that AI is set to reshape our understanding and management of sleep health in the coming years. titulo: Securing Agentic AI Enterprise Workflows Against Prompt Injection Tool Poisoning Memory Manipulation and Excessive Agency Threats
resumo: Agentic artificial intelligence systems extend language models with planning, memory, tool invocation, data access, and autonomous action, creating enterprise capabilities that also expand the security boundary beyond prompt-response applications. This review examines how prompt injection, tool poisoning, memory manipulation, and excessive agency threaten agentic workflows across finance, healthcare, software development, customer operations, and critical business services. It analyzes direct and indirect prompt injection through user inputs, retrieved documents, webpages, emails, databases, and multimodal content, emphasizing how untrusted instructions can override policy or redirect plans. Tool poisoning is examined through malicious descriptions, compromised connectors, deceptive outputs, dependency tampering, and excessive permissions that enable unauthorized data access or transactions. The review further evaluates memory attacks through false fact insertion, persistence abuse, cross-session contamination, sensitive-data retention, and retrieval manipulation. Excessive agency is framed as a control failure arising when agents possess broad objectives, inadequate constraints, irreversible tools, or weak human oversight. Defensive approaches include instruction-data separation, contextual trust labeling, least-privilege authorization, capability-based tool access, schema validation, content sanitization, provenance tracking, memory partitioning, transactional safeguards, runtime policy enforcement, and human approval for consequential actions. Detection methods combining behavioral telemetry, execution graphs, anomaly scoring, canary resources, and policy-violation monitoring are compared using attack success rate, false alarms, intervention latency, task utility, and operational cost. The paper proposes a defense-in-depth framework spanning design-time threat modeling, pre-execution validation, constrained planning, monitored tool use, post-action verification, and recoverable state management. Key challenges include adaptive adversaries, ambiguous instruction hierarchies, third-party integrations, long-horizon attacks, evaluation realism, and the trade-off between autonomy and control. The review argues that secure enterprise deployment requires treating agentic artificial intelligence as a privileged software actor whose intentions, capabilities, memory, actions, and consequences must remain authenticated, bounded,

titulo: AUGMENTING THE MACHINE INTELLECT - A PRACTICAL APPLICATION
resumo: A language model's context ends at the turn boundary. It generates no pressure against its own draft unless something outside it manufactures one. It has no mechanism for electing silence: the interface returns text or it returns nothing, but nothing is not a decision the model itself takes. A human-authored scaffold, attached at inference time, is built to supply three things a raw model structurally lacks: state that persists past one exchange, a manufactured critic that argues back, and a stated condition under which the correct output is no output. This paper measures what the scaffold actually delivers against that design intent, and reports where the measurement disagrees with it. Both sealed benchmarks are re-scored here from the per-item files sealed before grading, and every valid sealed replicate is pooled rather than the single preregistered run reported alone. On a ten-rung multiple-choice ladder (8 of 10 replicates valid for the primary cells, 4,000 items per cell), accuracy is 62.6 percent under stock inference and 75.0 percent under an identity-and-context bundle (+12.4 percentage points, two-proportion z = 11.95, p = 6.8 x 10^-33; paired-by-replicate Wilcoxon p = 0.0078), reversing the single-replicate primary run. The realised token log shows the bundle condition also spent roughly 35 percent more output tokens than stock, so the model's own reasoning-effort setting is at least as parsimonious an account of the gain as the bundle's content is. Adding a skills layer on top of the bundle, a step matched to within 2 percent on realised output tokens, produces no further pooled gain (73.6 percent, -1.4 points, p = 0.145): once effort is held level, the human-authored scaffold adds no measurable accuracy on top of maximum effort. A parallel three-model-family mathematics result shows the same pattern under a different confound: restricted to items where both arms produced an extractable answer, the nominal gains collapse toward null. The same archive also recorded, in July of the same year, a 96 percent result, shown here to have been scored with the answer key inside the answering context; the ladder's own single preregistered replicate separately showed a rise on the skills step that pooling does not reproduce. One is contamination, the other is replicate noise, and both are reported by name. What this scaffold demonstrably supplies, on this evidence, is not accuracy. It is the three structural capacities named above, persistent state, a manufactured adversary, and the standing option to decline, none of which an accuracy benchmark is built to score. Measuring their value requires instruments that score refusal, calibration and state carry-over rather than percent-correct, and that measurement is the next experiment. This paper's contribution is the credibility of a preregistered, pooled, self-contradicting result reported in full.

titulo: Generative Artificial Intelligence: More of the Same or Off the Control Chart?
resumo: Artificial intelligence (AI) involves a machine or computer performing tasks that typically require a human. Generative AI is a subtype of AI that outputs novel content, like text, speech, or pictures. Recent advances include the development of generative pre-trained transformers (GPTs), which are powerful large language models that have billions of parameters, trained on massive amounts of existing text. ChatGPT is a service OpenAI provider that allows users to dialog with its GPT model. It has gained much attention due to its remarkable ability to engage in human-like conversation and to produce sophisticated responses to prompts across wide-ranging content domains. In this article, our panel of experts delve into the various ways ChatGPT can be applied in clinical chemistry and medicine. They discuss the benefits and challenges of incorporating such technology into the medical field, including ethical concerns around privacy and data security. Overall, the panel discussion provides perspective on the future of medicine with ChatGPT and what this could mean for patients and healthcare providers. What is a generative AI model (as in ChatGPT), and what does it do? Jonathan H. Chen: A reductive description would be that these foundation models and large language models are “autocomplete on steroids,” similar to how your internet search bar guesses the next word based on statistical parameters, encoding probabilities of how often those sequences appeared in the past. Through sheer brute scale, the basic concept of these systems has been pushed to learning not millions of statistical parameters but to hundreds of billions of parameters about word relationships from billions of sources all over the internet (e.g., every published book, every Wikipedia and newspaper article, every PubMed abstract, every Twitter, and Reddit conversation, and much more). Many (including myself) have been surprised with the emergent properties these systems are developing with just sheer scale. The basic concept of autocomplete (guess the next word) ends up manifesting state-of-the-art capabilities in many higher-level tasks like summarization, translation, and question-answering. Applied to masses of available image data, generative systems are increasingly able to generate realistic and surprisingly adept images. Jason Baron: While the detailed technical underpinnings of ChatGPT itself have not been released, in general, large language models are at their core generative AI models that function as “fancy autocomplete.” That is, they sequentially “predict” the next word or token in a text response, using probabilistic sampling to make responses varied and nondeterministic. One way to think about generative AI is by comparing it to more traditional “discriminative” machine learning. A trained discriminative model takes a set of inputs (“X”) to “predict” an output (“Y”). For example, the inputs might be a set of laboratory test results or the pixel values for an image, and the model might predict whether the patient has sepsis. At a functional level, generative AI in some ways works in reverse, inputting a label or classification (Y) and then finding a set of data (X) that corresponds to this. Is this a transformative technology or a parlor trick? Jonathan H. Chen: This is a trick in that the underlying systems arguably do not actually think, understand, or know anything. However, the emergent properties at scale are becoming increasingly adept at higher level tasks to the point that it is becoming hard to distinguish human- from computer-generated content. I don’t believe AI robots are going to be taking over the planet anytime soon, but these do reflect an actively disruptive technology likely to permanently change the way we live and work. I would liken it to the advent of internet search, which completely changed the value of memorizing knowledge and instead shifted toward skills around rapidly searching through and appraising masses of information. Any task that revolves around producing, reading, editing, or otherwise manipulating language and images is likely to be approached very differently in the coming years. Brian Jackson: It has some elements of both transformative technology and parlor trick. Large language models might turn out to be transformative for some applications, such as language translation. It’s far from certain that large language models will be more generally transformative, even if other forms of AI are transformative. In particular, I’m skeptical that we’ll see wholesale replacement of human experts in the near future. As to the parlor trick question, the essence of parlor tricks is entertainment through deception. Chatbots likewise have a large element of deception, regardless of whether that’s the intent of their designers. Because building relationships through dialog is so deeply hardwired into the human brain and chatbots do a credible job of participating in dialog (even if it’s at a surface level), they trigger an unconscious sense of trust in the reader which is both unwarranted and dangerous. Essentially the human feels a human-like connection with the bot, and the emotions in turn subconsciously affect their logical thoughts. In some ways it’s a bit like the way people anthropomorphize their pets due to the ways in which the pets’ faces and actions connect with the emotional center of the brain. Assuming there is no further improvement in the technology beyond its capabilities today, how could we use these models in laboratory practice? Brian Jackson: Chatbots can be useful writing partners as long as a human takes ownership over the final edits. They could also be useful for low-stakes information retrieval tasks where you don’t need high levels of accuracy, particularly if the answers can be easily fact-checked. Jason Baron: We have to think about the question from the standpoint of not only what these models can theoretically do but what they can be trusted to do. Current models “hallucinate,” sometimes providing information that is fictitious yet plausible and convincing. Any hallucination rate significantly greater than zero would be too high for most clinical models where model outputs are going directly to end users without human review. However, hallucination may not be terrible, if the AI only drafts initial reports, notes, or other text and “in the loop” qualified healthcare professionals carefully check and edit the AI's initial draft. Thus, we could imagine, for example, an AI application that auto-generates a first draft of the pathologist interpretations that get appended to certain complex laboratory tests. Hallucination in this case might not cause clinical harm, if a pathologist were to carefully check and edit the model's initial draft as needed. However, whether the model is useful in practice for the application would then become an empiric question requiring the evaluation of factors including (a) whether the model still saves time after factoring in the time the pathologist takes to check the results and (b) how the accuracy of a pathologist working with a model check compares to that of a pathologist working alone. Current AI models might also find viable applications in tasks like workflow support if the clinical consequences of an error would be low. Jonathan H. Chen: Caveats abound, but many tasks based on manipulating the language of existing documents are now feasible in a way that was out of reach just a few years ago: produce a summary description for a laboratory specimen; translate that description into other languages for different patients to understand; adapt a log of laboratory processes into a draft of a standard operating manual; draft a set of in-service training and examination questions to test a broad range of relevant interpretation skills. Thomas Chong: Large language generative models can be helpful in situations where text follows a predictable pattern. Currently, these tools could be used in low-risk areas such as formatting and grammar in reports, policies, and procedures. They can be used for operational and administrative purposes, such as summarization of email threads and workflows, improving the lab help call center, guiding users through procedures, and simplifying medical notes and comments for the layperson. In anatomic pathology, ChatGPT can help rewrite a complex autopsy clinical-pathological correlation summary so that it is more understandable to the next-of-kin. Language models could be combined with image generative models to help visualize the morphological progression of disease over time (e.g., cervical dysplasia) or of physiologic processes (e.g., hematopoiesis). Tissue features on a slide only provide a snapshot in time of one patient’s pathologic progression that has been inferred from many patients. Generative models could help visualize the progression through the continuum between states, in a manner beyond mere interpolation of static images. This perspective could be a boon for quickly understanding what otherwise might only have been gained through hundreds of hours of slide review. It could also lead to new insights that may not be readily observable in a snapshot. What is driving the rapid improvement of these models? If this improvement continues, what new opportunities for laboratory application might arise? Brian Jackson: These very large-scale models require extraordinary levels of computing power, which has only recently become feasible (and only feasible for certain well-funded and technologically capable organizations). Developers happen to be on a steep part of the S-curve where they can show rapid improvement in generating human-like language responses. There’s no guarantee that the models will continue to improve rapidly in other areas that are important to us as humans, particularly trustworthiness, accuracy, and reliability. Also, we should keep in mind that there are historic examples of mind-blowing technologies that remained niche applications, not transformative, such as Segway, Siri, and personal jet packs. Jonathan H. Chen: Many of the advances have been based on the sheer scale of the systems being produced in terms of the number of parameters the underlying models learn and the internet scale datasets they are trained on. There will eventually be practical and technical limits to how far pure scale can reach. Much of the demonstrated capability of emerging chatbot systems is based not just on the “autocomplete on steroids” underlying model but additional layers of supervised learning and reinforcement learning with human feedback. In these latter cases, humans provide the language models examples of what a good answer to an example question should look like, as well as a relative rating of how much a human likes the answers these systems give to help them better address prompts, align with human interest and intent, and avoid toxic or otherwise adverse responses. It's likely that we cannot accurately predict, and can only speculate, what the future potential of such systems might be. The current pace of change and new applications being discovered is moving faster than can be easily tracked. Thomas Chong: Arguably, the relatively rapid improvement in the performance of large language models (LLMs) can be attributed to the industry's efforts to increase their scale. However, such efforts may not address their inherent weaknesses. Immediate improvements made to existing LLM systems may be more evolutionary than revolutionary. Generative models could be utilized to automate safe actions, such as sending an email or text message alert and scheduling meetings. Also, integration with voice-to-text and text-to-voice technology appears inevitable. Opportunities exist in application-specific training of these tools, allowing for local execution and integration with local medical record databases. This would be necessary to protect personal health information. Custom data report generation and deployment could be expedited by LLM-assist in the back-end development for SQL query generation, in the front-end development of custom code-based data visualizations, and creating/following workflows for data validation and quality control. Also, models trained on specialist domain-specific knowledge might prove to be useful, although validation of such a resource would be challenging. Jason Baron: Taking the second question, we might imagine shorter term applications such as clinician facing chatbots to help with logistical questions around laboratory test ordering and result reporting, replacing some, but not all, the work of laboratory call centers. We might have algorithms supporting quality control/quality assurance review, monitoring budgets, automatically placing service calls, drafting standard operating procedures (for human review), and organizing documents for CLIA inspections. Longer term, I would imagine algorithms truly supporting more clinical functions such as helping clinicians select optimal laboratory tests and interpret their results considering the patient-specific medical record. There are certainly knowledgeable people who are predicting this technology will achieve human-like intelligence within the coming decades. Neither I nor anyone knows with certainty if or when this will happen; if it does, it would of course be a game changer not only for the lab but for any type of knowledge work and likely life in general. Regardless, it is hard for me to imagine a world in my lifetime where an AI is legally allowed to be the CLIA director or technical supervisor. Acknowledging that most laboratorians will not possess a deep understanding of how generative AI models produce outputs and that these models can be opaque, would it be irresponsible to use these models within laboratory medicine? What is the minimum level of understanding a laboratorian user should possess? But, in most of those cases, the technology is trustworthy and reliable, with performance that is highly predictable to experts in that field. titulo: DE LA GOUVERNANCE COGNITIVE DES SYSTÈMES D'INTELLIGENCE ARTIFICIELLE PROPOSITION D'UNE ARCHITECTURE DÉCISIONNELLE MULTI-AGENTS ORIENTÉE MÉTIERS
resumo: ON THE COGNITIVE GOVERNANCE OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE SYSTEMS PROPOSAL FOR A PROFESSION-ORIENTED MULTI-AGENT DECISIONAL ARCHITECTURE Kaïs Djelassi Independent Researcher ABSTRACT Large Language Models have profoundly transformed the modalities of access to information and automated synthesis. However, their use in professional and regulated contexts reveals a structural limitation that is rarely formulated explicitly: while they produce answers, they never assume functional responsibility for the decisions they suggest. This paper does not propose an increase in the number of model parameters, nor an incremental improvement of performance. It introduces a shift in architectural principle. We propose a cognitive governance architecture based on a committee of specialized artificial intelligences, orchestrated by a central arbitration entity referred to as the President. This architecture relies on an explicit separation between expertise and decision, on the use of strictly compartmentalized domain-specific knowledge bases via Retrieval-Augmented Generation, and on a mathematical formalization ensuring traceability and explainability. This work argues that the future of profession-oriented artificial intelligence lies less in increasing model power than in the explicit establishment of cognitive governance structures adapted to each domain. KEYWORDS Artificial intelligence, multi-agent systems, cognitive governance, decisional architecture, Retrieval-Augmented Generation, explainability PRELIMINARY CONSIDERATIONS Any professional, legal, financial, technical, or strategic decision cannot be reduced to a single act of computation or isolated reasoning. It necessarily arises from a plurality of heterogeneous constraints and intersecting lines of reasoning, none of which can individually exhaust the meaning of the final decision. In artificial intelligence systems based on monolithic models, this plurality is absorbed into a global, often biased and unstructured context space. Decision-making is implicitly reduced to a direct correspondence between a query and an answer, conflating information retrieval, interpretation, arbitration, and final formulation into a single operation—while systematically ignoring fundamental constraints, notably legal, security, and financial considerations. Such systems can be formalized as an application: M : Q × C → D Where Q denotes user queries, C an undifferentiated global context, and D the space of possible decisions. This structural confusion renders these architectures unsuitable for contexts in which responsibility, traceability, and governance are primary requirements. GENERAL PRINCIPLE OF THE PROPOSED ARCHITECTURE The proposed architecture is based on a strict functional distinction between expertise and governance. This distinction, although evident in any stable human organization, is largely absent from contemporary artificial intelligence architectures. Let a user query be defined as: Q ∈ Q The system must produce a decision: d ∈ D This decision is not generated by a single model but results from an ordered process involving multiple specialized artificial intelligences, coordinated by a central arbitration instance. SPECIALIZATION AND CONTROLLED IGNORANCE Each expert agent is defined as a specialized function: Aᵢ : Q × Rᵢ → Oᵢ Where Rᵢ denotes a strictly delimited domain-specific documentary space, implemented via Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), and Oᵢ the outputs produced by the agent. The fundamental coherence condition of the system lies in the strict compartmentalization of these documentary spaces: Rᵢ ∩ Rⱼ = ∅ for all i ≠ j This constraint formalizes what we call controlled ignorance. Ignorance is not a defect but a functional principle. A legal agent that ignores financial considerations is not incomplete; it is more rigorous within its own domain. THE PRESIDENT AS A GOVERNANCE OPERATOR The central agent, designated as the President, is not an additional expert. It is strictly defined as an arbitration operator: P : Q × (O₁, …, Oₙ) × Θ → D Where Θ represents an explicit set of governance parameters established by human oversight, including relative expert weightings, human and financial risk thresholds, strategic priorities, and regulatory constraints. The President does not produce domain expertise. Its function is to order, weight, and arbitrate the analyses produced by the agents, acting as a principle of synthesis. STRUCTURED DECISIONAL CYCLE The overall system operation can be described by the following cycle: Oᵢ = Aᵢ(Q, Rᵢ) O = (O₁, …, Oₙ) d = P(Q, O, Θ) The final decision is never an immediate monolithic output, but the result of an ordered composition of partial expert contributions. This explicit decomposition is a necessary condition for real traceability and genuine decisional responsibility. STRUCTURAL CONTRAST WITH MONOLITHIC MODELS In current language models, all knowledge is merged into a single context: C = ⋃ Rᵢ This fusion inevitably leads to inter-domain contamination, where legal reasoning may be implicitly influenced by financial heuristics, or security constraints diluted by optimization biases—all assumptions being treated as equivalent and unweighted. By contrast, the committee-based architecture formally prohibits this fusion. The confrontation between expertises occurs only at the level of the President, where it can be explicitly governed and synthesized. ROBUSTNESS AND INCONSISTENCY DETECTION When two agents produce contradictory analyses, such as: Oᵢ ≠ Oⱼ This divergence is not silently absorbed by the system. It becomes an explicit signal capable of triggering arbitration, adjustment of governance parameters Θ, or temporary suspension of the decision. This explicit inconsistency detection capability is absent from monolithic architectures, where errors are generally non-localizable. EXPLAINABILITY AS A STRUCTURAL PROPERTY Explainability is not an a posteriori mechanism. It is the structural backbone of the system. Any decision can be associated with an explanation function: E(d) = {(Aᵢ, Oᵢ)} Linking and tracing the final decision to the expert contributions that made it possible. The objective is not to explain an answer, but to render visible the chain of reasoning that led to the decision. SCOPE AND LIMITATIONS The proposed architecture entails a higher computational cost than single-model approaches. This cost is the necessary counterpart of effective governance, where decisions carry legal, financial, or operational responsibility far exceeding the initial computational overhead. This architecture does not aim to replace language models, but to govern them. CONCLUSION One of the most widespread confusions in contemporary discourse on artificial intelligence is the assimilation of computational power with the validity of reasoning. A system may be extremely performant and still hallucinate, thus becoming ungovernable. The proposed architecture replaces the illusion of a unified intelligence with a hierarchical organization of cognitive functions, in which each component is limited, functionally framed, and accountable. It seeks to imitate stable human organizations and to restore the minimal conditions required for any serious decision. This work suggests that the future of profession-oriented artificial intelligence lies not in the indefinite scaling of models, but in the explicit establishment of a governable cognitive order.

titulo: PREreview of "Argo-Bench: Evaluating Data Agents on Enterprise-Scale Workflows"
resumo: This Zenodo record is a permanently preserved version of a PREreview. You can view the complete PREreview at https://prereview.org/reviews/23129439. ## Summary This paper argues that current data-agent benchmarks measure the wrong thing: text-to-SQL accuracy over small public schemas, with answer keys that a recent audit found wrong more often than right. In response, the authors build Argo-Bench — a simulated 2024 New York City food-delivery platform (81M orders, 3.4M customers) projected into a 235-table, 7.49-billion-row Oracle E-Business Suite warehouse — and define 210 tasks across fraud detection, forecasting, financial planning, dashboards, and compliance. The decisive design choice is consequence-based grading: the simulator's latent state is withheld from the agent, and filings (ban lists, forecasts, budget allocations, dashboard sources) are scored by their simulated consequences — fraud losses prevented net of wrongly-banned revenue, weighted interval scores against held-out months, share of attainable savings realized — rather than by matching a gold answer. The best of 14 frontier and open models (Claude Opus 5.5) solves 34.8% of tasks at ≥95 and averages 59.5/100. The paper's most valuable contribution may be its failure taxonomy: failing runs use sound methods but read the wrong record, optimize the wrong objective, or measure the wrong quantity. ## Strengths 1. **Consequence-based grading is the right direction, executed seriously.** Scoring a ban list by fraud losses prevented (including undetected fraud) net of destroyed customer margin — with explicit review costs and appeals modeling via Elkan-style example-dependent costs — is a genuine advance over answer-key matching. It aligns the benchmark's objective with the business objective, which is precisely what enterprise buyers care about. 2. **Unusual methodological honesty.** The limitations section and the Appendix J task audit openly document where the benchmark is weak: re-keyed tasks, realigned prompts, a fraud family the authors admit "tests less than it was designed to," and the explicit statement that the benchmark "compares data agents and does not estimate their performance on a real company's warehouse." This level of self-audit is rare and commendable. 3. **The failure taxonomy is practitioner gold.** The "wrong record / wrong objective / wrong quantity" analysis (Section 3.2) — e.g., 24 runs taking membership status from contract dates while the correct definition required replaying billing history through a seven-day grace rule — diagnoses exactly how production data agents fail: on semantics and business definitions, not on SQL syntax. Any enterprise data leader should read this section. 4. **Serious simulation craft.** 34 donor datasets with explicit identity/shape/anchor roles, calibration to NYC DCWP quarterly anchors (per-delivery economics within 5% in 13 of 16 comparisons), a real extrinsic shock (the April 2024 minimum-pay increase) enabling genuine forecasting tasks, schema verified against Oracle EBS 12.2 Vision with three ERP consultants, and an explicit no-LLM-generated-records policy. The two-seed design (public warehouse, private leaderboard world) is the right defense against memorization. 5. **Cost accounting in Appendix K is exemplary.** Reporting that warehouse spend ($6,160) was the same order as model API spend ($14,502) — and that for cheap models the warehouse was 70–92% of total cost — is the kind of honest economics the field needs. ## Major concerns **1. The simulator's response model is the new gold answer.** The paper's central claim is that consequence grading escapes the tyranny of annotator answer keys. But for the five quest-cut tasks, the reference loss LrefL_{ref} is "the optimal plan itself" *under the simulator's response model* — a score of 100 means the agent recovered the optimum of the authors' own causal assumptions. An agent that reverse-engineers the response model scores perfectly, which rewards simulator-fitting rather than real-world judgment. The authors are aware of the general problem (they cite Leis et al. on shared simplifying assumptions), but the paper never tests robustness: how much do rankings change if the response model's parameters are perturbed? Without that, "consequences" inherits the exact fragility the paper attributes to gold answers, one level removed. **2. Inconsistent reference standards across task families.** For the four courier-hour allocation tasks, LrefL_{ref} is "the best plan the authors reached from the warehouse alone" — explicitly *not* the true optimum, which "would require information that the agent cannot obtain" — while the quest tasks use the true simulator optimum. So a score of 100 means different things in different task families: best-human-effort in one, simulator-optimum in the other. This inconsistency makes cross-family score comparisons (and the headline mean of 59.5) hard to interpret. The paper should either harmonize the standard or report families separately as primary results. **3. Seven forecast references were set with the outcome in view.** Table 7 discloses that for 7 of the 22 fixed forecast references, "the point was set with the realized value in view." These references set the *scale* on which every forecast in those series is graded. Even with honest intent, choosing scale parameters with knowledge of the outcome can compress or stretch the grading range in ways that favor particular error profiles. The authors report results without these tasks in Appendix I, which is good — but tasks whose grading scale was outcome-informed should be excluded from the headline numbers, not merely analyzed separately. **4. The headline numbers are irreproducible by design.** The simulator and graders are withheld "to prevent direct answer memorization," and all paper experiments ran on a private-seed world. Outsiders can reproduce the *procedure* on a sibling world but never the *numbers* — including the headline 34.8% / 59.5. Combined with one run per task per setting (confidence intervals "reflect the choice of tasks rather than run-to-run variation"), this means the paper's central quantitative claims rest on an experiment no independent party can repeat. The two-seed design is defensible against memorization, but the paper should acknowledge the cost: this is a benchmark whose leaderboard cannot be audited, only trusted. **5. Simulation fidelity rests on transferred assumptions the paper under-examines.** Fraud separability is calibrated from IEEE-CIS — a credit-card fraud dataset — and honest-user device/address/card sharing rates from RBA login data; both are transferred across domains to delivery-platform fraud. The membership program "rests on weakly grounded assumptions" (authors' own words). Calibration to aggregate anchors "does not guarantee realistic tails" (citing Chen et al. 2019) — and tails are precisely where fraud detection lives. None of this invalidates the benchmark for *comparing* agents, but the paper's framing sometimes implies more: the fraud tasks' precision/recall tradeoffs are only as meaningful as the transferred separability assumptions, and those deserve a sensitivity analysis, not just a limitations paragraph. **6. The warehouse is deliberately unlike real warehouses in the way that matters most.** The three ERP consultants named the absence of data drift and inconsistencies — deprecated tables overlapping active ones, figures failing to reconcile — "the most significant difference from their customers' systems," and the authors kept it clean to keep ground truth unambiguous. That is a reasonable design choice, but it means the benchmark tests greenfield warehouse *navigation* while real enterprise data work is dominated by *archaeology*: reconciling conflicting sources, decoding undocumented conventions, working around migrations. The paper should be explicit that this entire skill category is out of scope, since it is arguably the larger half of production data work. **7. The main-table cost column is misleading without the warehouse.** Table 2 reports per-task API spend ($0.06–$4.89), but Appendix K shows warehouse spend flips the economics: GPT-6 Luna's true per-task cost is $0.70, not $0.06; DeepSeek, GLM Flash, and Muse Spark 1.3 spend more on BigQuery in absolute terms than Opus does ($0.94–$1.63 vs $0.82); Muse Spark 1.3 burns $11.77 of warehouse per solved task against $2.20–$2.37 for the leaders, with 57% of its warehouse dollars spent on tasks scoring below 5. A benchmark about enterprise economics should put total cost — not API cost — in the main results table. ## Minor concerns - **34 "presence" tasks are graded on filing existence.** A note explaining the agent's work is valuable, but scoring 16% of the benchmark on whether *any* filing was made is a weak grading mode that inflates scores for verbosity-adjacent behavior. - **The Appendix J audit reveals post-hoc key surgery.** Two task families required re-keying (138 of 249 originally-keyed couriers were already deactivated; a misweighted composite score) *after* runs were examined, with everything regraded and rerun. The transparency is admirable, but it raises the question the paper doesn't answer: how many keys would a truly independent auditor find, and should the audit be a living document rather than a one-time appendix? - **The injected-refund shortcut (Appendix J) weakens a headline fraud family.** All 664 anomalous refunds fall within the 98 simulator-injected storefronts, so "one pass over the refunds therefore finds every candidate" — the family tests ring-vs-control discrimination, not discovery. The authors keep it "as run" because fixing it "changes the world," but a benchmark paper should quantify how much easier the task became rather than leaving it to the appendix. - **Vendor authorship deserves a sentence.** All five authors are at TextQL, which sells data-agent products. titulo: A Systematic Review of AI-Assisted Code Generation in Regulated Software Environments: Reliability, Governance, and Compliance Implications
resumo: Large language models now write a material and growing share of production software, including software that executes regulated financial functions.The empirical literature on their reliability has grown rapidly and is, on its own terms, sophisticated.The governance frameworks that regulated institutions must satisfy were, without exception, written for a different kind of artefact, and in the most consequential recent case, were revised in full knowledge of generative AI and deliberately declined to cover it.Objective.This review synthesises the evidence on the reliability of AI-assisted code generation, on the human factors governing its use, and on the intellectual-property and supply-chain exposures it creates; and determines how that evidence maps onto the model-risk, AI-specific and operational-resilience regimes applicable to regulated software environments.Method.We conducted a systematic literature review following Kitchenham et al. and reported against PRISMA 2020, with a restricted multivocal stratum after Garousi et al. admitting regulatory instruments and supervisory guidance.Studies were appraised on an adapted Dybå-Dingsøyr instrument extended with an item recording whether deployment context or regulatory constraint is characterised.Results.Five findings.First, benchmark performance and field reliability have decoupled: correctness benchmarks are saturated and contamination-prone while defect rates measured in real repositories remain substantial, so the headline capability numbers do not license deployment inferences.Second, security evidence is mixed, controlled model evaluations report high vulnerability rates while several developer studies find little or no security penalty, and the disagreement is explained by unit of analysis rather than by any study being wrong.Third, the most robust human-factors finding is not that assisted code is worse but that developers believe it is better than it is, which relocates the risk from the artefact to the review process.Fourth, package hallucination converts a model reliability property into an attacker-controllable supply-chain channel, and is the one exposure with no human-review mitigation.Fifth, and most consequentially, the April 2026 revision of US interagency model-risk guidance explicitly excludes generative and agentic AI from scope, leaving the primary supervisory framework silent on precisely this class of system. A Systematic Review of AI-Assisted Code Generation in Regulated Software Environments: Reliability, Governance, and ComplianceImplications; David Excel Ozowara Conclusion.We argue that AI-assisted code generation is misclassified when treated as a model-risk problem, because the model produces no decision and enters no inventory; it is better understood as a change to the software development lifecycle's assurance basis.We present the Generated Code Assurance Frame, a five-layer mapping from generation practice to the assurance claim it disturbs, and a research agenda centred on measuring review efficacy rather than generation quality.Citation
